_doc: FIX-1113 — the allow-list for public routines anon/authenticated may EXECUTE.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. Supabase grants EXECUTE to anon AND authenticated on
every newly created function by default (FIX-695, FIX-834). So a routine
becomes callable via POST /rest/v1/rpc/<name> the moment it is created,
unless its migration carries an explicit REVOKE — and a CREATE OR REPLACE
that drops-and-recreates re-opens a grant that was previously closed. That
is not hypothetical: FIX-1111 re-opened one on a sibling procedure, and
auditing the fallout is how FIX-1113 was found.
The weekly integrity audit diffs prod against this file and reports
ADDITIONS as warnings. It is REPORT-ONLY by design — it never blocks a
build and never auto-revokes, because a wrong auto-revoke silently breaks
a page and a wrong warning costs a minute of reading.
WHEN THE AUDIT WARNS. Classify before revoking (FIX-834's rule): find who
actually calls it. A route/client caller means it belongs here — add it to
the right bucket in the same PR that added the routine. No caller, or only
pg_cron/service_role callers, means it wants
REVOKE ALL ON FUNCTION public.f(...) FROM PUBLIC, anon, authenticated;
GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION public.f(...) TO service_role;
in a migration.
THE RULE THAT FELL OUT OF SEEDING THIS (FIX-1113): no PROCEDURE belongs in
any bucket. Every prokind='p' routine on this platform is a heavy pipeline
procedure driven by pg_cron as postgres. All 13 that carried an anon grant
were revoked in migration 20260828000000; the newer ones already had it
right. If a procedure ever shows up in the audit's additions, it is drift.
Names only, no argument lists: overloads share a grant posture here, and a
signature change should not read as a new finding.
Seeded 2026-08-28 from prod, post-revoke: 69 routines.
